content: Diastasis recti is a condition characterized by the separation of the rectus abdominis muscle into two halves, specifically the right and left portions. Under normal circumstances, the two sides of the rectus abdominis muscle are joined at the midline by a connective tissue structure called the linea alba. However, diastasis recti occurs when this connection is disrupted, leading to a separation of the muscle. This condition is most commonly observed in two distinct populations: newborns and pregnant women. In newborns, the rectus abdominis muscle may not be fully developed or sealed at the midline, which can result in diastasis recti. This is more frequently seen in premature infants and African American newborns. In pregnant or postpartum women, the separation of the rectus abdominis muscle is caused by the stretching of the abdominal wall due to the growing uterus. This condition is more prevalent in women who have had multiple pregnancies, as repeated episodes of abdominal stretching increase the likelihood of developing diastasis recti. In some cases, during pregnancy, the uterus may visibly bulge through the abdominal wall beneath the skin. Clinically, diastasis recti presents as a ridge or bulge running along the midline of the abdomen, extending from the xiphoid process (the lower part of the sternum) to the umbilicus (navel). This ridge becomes more pronounced when the individual strains or engages the abdominal muscles and may disappear when the abdominal muscles are relaxed. During relaxation, the medial borders of the separated right and left halves of the rectus abdominis muscle can often be palpated. The diagnosis of diastasis recti is typically made through a physical examination. To rule out other conditions, such as a ventral hernia, imaging studies like ultrasound may be utilized. Treatment is generally not required for pregnant women while they are still carrying their child. However, complications can arise, such as the development of an umbilical or ventral hernia in children, though this is rare. If such hernias occur, they can usually be corrected surgically. In some cases, diastasis recti may also occur in older individuals or those with weakened abdominal musculature. The midline separation or hernia becomes more apparent with activities or maneuvers that increase intra-abdominal pressure, such as straining or coughing.
